knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For \(\min_x f(x)\) subject to \(c(x)=0\), let \(J_k=\nabla c(x_k)\), \(L(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\lambda^{\mathsf T}c(x)\), and let \(B_k\) be a symmetric approximation to \(\nabla_{xx}^2L(x_k,\lambda_k)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth equality constraints and local step computation in \(d\)-space. The nonlinear constraints are replaced by their affine linearization in the subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linearly constrained Lagrangian interface is the subproblem \(\min_{d\in\mathbb R^n} m_k(d):=\nabla f(x_k)^{\mathsf T}d+(1/2)d^{\mathsf T}B_kd+(\rho_k/2)\|c(x_k)+J_kd\|_2^2\) subject to \(c(x_k)+J_kd=0\), or, equivalently on that affine set, minimization of the Lagrangian quadratic model \(\nabla f(x_k)^{\mathsf T}d+(1/2)d^{\mathsf T}B_kd\). The interface consists of using augmentation in the surrounding merit or stabilization model while enforcing the linearized constraint explicitly in the step subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interface forms a step by replacing the nonlinear equality constraint with its affine linearization. The trial step minimizes a Lagrangian quadratic model over that affine set. A quadratic residual augmentation may be retained in the written objective or surrounding merit model, but it vanishes on every exactly feasible linearized step; its role is therefore stabilization or globalization outside the exact affine feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(c\) are continuously differentiable, and the quadratic model uses a symmetric matrix \(B_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The step is defined by a Lagrangian quadratic objective together with the explicit linearized constraint \(c(x_k)+J_kd=0\); augmentation does not change objective values within that affine set.
equivalent_formulations_latex: On \(c(x_k)+J_kd=0\), \((\rho_k/2)\|c(x_k)+J_kd\|_2^2=0\), so the augmented and unaugmented quadratic models have identical constrained minimizers.
The KKT conditions are \(B_kd+\nabla f(x_k)+J_k^{\mathsf T}\nu=0\) and \(c(x_k)+J_kd=0\).
special_cases_latex: If \(c(x)=Ax-b\) is affine, the linearized constraint is the original constraint at \(x_k+d\).
With \(B_k=\nabla_{xx}^2L(x_k,\lambda_k)\), the model is the classical equality-constrained Newton/SQP quadratic model.
immediate_consequences_latex: Exact satisfaction of the linearized constraint removes the quadratic violation term from the subproblem objective.
An infeasible linearized constraint requires a relaxed, elastic, or least-squares variant.
boundary_notes: This definition does not cover inequality working sets or complementarity constraints.
If the augmentation is intended to affect the step directly, the affine constraint must be relaxed rather than imposed exactly.

knowledge_statements.title: Penalty-Free Primal–Dual Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between augmented-Lagrangian models and primal–dual methods using the ordinary Lagrangian only.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For equality constraints \(c(x)=0\), a penalty-free primal–dual step is formed from the ordinary Lagrangian \(L(x,y)=f(x)+y^{\mathsf T}c(x)\) and the KKT residual \(F(x,y)=(\nabla_xL(x,y),c(x))\), with no term \((\rho/2)\lVert c(x)\rVert^2\) in its model or merit mechanism. Its Newton equation is \(F'(x_k,y_k)(d_k,\delta y_k)=-F(x_k,y_k)\). This is the structural boundary: adding a positive quadratic residual term produces an augmented model, whereas multiplier updates and primal–dual coupling alone do not constitute augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal–dual method is penalty-free when its model uses only the ordinary Lagrangian and KKT equations, without a quadratic constraint-residual term.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(c\) are twice differentiable where the Newton equation is used.
The equality-constrained KKT residual is well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Absence of every positive term \((\rho/2)\lVert c(x)\rVert^2\) separates this interface from augmented-Lagrangian modeling.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For a smooth equality-constrained problem, define the KKT residual \(F(x,\lambda)=(\nabla f(x)+J(x)^{\mathsf T}\lambda,c(x))\). Let \(z_k=(x_k,\lambda_k)\) and let \(p_k=(d_k,\delta\lambda_k)\) be a primal-dual direction.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth equality constraints. Penalty-free means that neither direction generation nor acceptance uses a tunable positive multiple of a squared constraint violation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A penalty-free primal-dual interface is an iteration in which \(p_k\) is computed directly from the Lagrangian KKT equations, for example \(DF(z_k)p_k=-F(z_k)+e_k\), and the update \(z_{k+1}=z_k+\alpha_kp_k\) is controlled by residual, filter, or feasibility–optimality conditions that introduce no term \((\rho/2)\|c(x)\|_2^2\) with tunable \(\rho>0\). The interface with ALM is the parameter boundary \(\rho=0\), where \(\mathcal L_0(x,\lambda)=L(x,\lambda)\), together with the absence of the residual multiplier step \(\lambda^+=\lambda+\rho c(x^+)\) as an augmentation mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A penalty-free primal-dual method computes directions directly from the Lagrangian KKT equations and globalizes them through residual, filter, or separate feasibility and optimality tests without adding a tunable squared constraint penalty. It meets the augmented-Lagrangian family at the zero-augmentation boundary, but it does not use the scaled-residual multiplier update as its defining mechanism.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(c\) are continuously differentiable; Newton instances require the derivatives defining \(DF\).
The linear-solve residual \(e_k\) and acceptance rule are explicitly specified.
No positive quadratic-augmentation parameter is used in direction generation or acceptance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Penalty-free status is characterized by KKT-based primal-dual updates with \(\rho=0\) and no tunable quadratic constraint-violation term.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The objective identity at the interface is \(\mathcal L_0(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\lambda^{\mathsf T}c(x)=L(x,\lambda)\).
special_cases_latex: A primal-dual Newton method using the norm \(\|F(z)\|_2\) for line-search acceptance is penalty-free under this definition.
A filter method comparing feasibility and optimality without combining them through a penalty weight is also penalty-free.
immediate_consequences_latex: A method does not become augmented merely because its KKT system contains multipliers.
Introducing \((\rho/2)\|c\|^2\) with \(\rho>0\) moves the method outside the penalty-free interface.
boundary_notes: Barrier parameters used for inequality interiors are not quadratic penalty parameters, but inequality-constrained variants require a separate complementarity formulation.
A fixed norm weighting of the KKT residual must be distinguished from an augmented-Lagrangian penalty parameter.

notation.meaning: Zero-augmentation boundary between ordinary and augmented Lagrangians.

knowledge_statements.title: SQP Globalization Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Use of an augmented-Lagrangian merit function to globalize equality-constrained SQP steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At \((x_k,y_k)\), compute an SQP step \(d_k\) by minimizing \(\nabla f(x_k)^{\mathsf T}d+(1/2)d^{\mathsf T}B_kd\) subject to \(c(x_k)+J_c(x_k)d=0\), and obtain the subproblem multiplier \(\widehat y_{k+1}\). Choose \(\rho_k>0\) and test \(x_k+\alpha d_k\) using an augmented-Lagrangian merit function \(\mathcal L_{\rho_k}(x,y_k)\), possibly with a compatible multiplier path. Backtrack until the prescribed sufficient decrease holds, then set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kd_k\) and update \(y_{k+1}\) from \(\widehat y_{k+1}\). Stop when feasibility and Lagrangian-stationarity residuals satisfy tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interface computes an SQP step from a linearly constrained quadratic model and globalizes it using augmented-Lagrangian merit decrease.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(c\) are continuously differentiable; second-order models use a symmetric \(B_k\).
The linearized SQP constraints are consistent or are handled by a restoration variant.
The merit test and multiplier path are chosen consistently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each accepted SQP step satisfies the selected augmented-Lagrangian globalization test before the primal and multiplier iterates are updated.

children.title: Newton–SQP Transition Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes marking transitions between Newton-like multiplier methods and SQP architectures.

knowledge_statements.title: Newton–SQP Transition Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions for switching between globalized SQP steps and full local primal–dual Newton steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) and \(c:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), define \(L(x,y)=f(x)+y^{\mathsf T}c(x)\), and set \(F(x,y)=(\nabla_xL(x,y),c(x))\). Fix \(\eta>0\) and \(M>0\). A safeguarded method may switch from globalized SQP to a full primal–dual Newton step at iteration \(k\) when \(\lVert F(x_k,y_k)\rVert\le\eta\), the KKT matrix \(F'(x_k,y_k)\) is nonsingular with \(\lVert F'(x_k,y_k)^{-1}\rVert\le M\), and the full Newton trial passes the globalization acceptance test; otherwise it retains safeguarded SQP or restoration. If \((x_*,y_*)\) satisfies \(F(x_*,y_*)=0\), \(F'(x_*,y_*)\) is nonsingular, \(F'\) is locally Lipschitz, \(M>\lVert F'(x_*,y_*)^{-1}\rVert\), and the globalization rule accepts full Newton steps sufficiently near \((x_*,y_*)\), then all three switch tests hold in a sufficiently small neighborhood. When the SQP subproblem uses the exact Lagrangian Hessian and the same constraint linearization, its primal step and multiplier change solve the same linear system as the primal–dual Newton correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A method may switch from safeguarded SQP to full Newton steps only when the KKT residual is small, the KKT matrix satisfies a chosen inverse bound, and the full step is accepted. Near a regular solution these tests persist only when the inverse threshold is chosen with margin and the globalization rule has local unit-step acceptance; exact-Hessian SQP then produces the same primal and multiplier correction as Newton's method.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(c\) are twice continuously differentiable near the target KKT point.
\(F'\) is locally Lipschitz, and \(F'(x_*,y_*)\) is nonsingular.
The globalization rule accepts sufficiently near full Newton steps.
The SQP model uses the exact Lagrangian Hessian and the same constraint linearization when step coincidence is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the stated local regularity, threshold, and acceptance assumptions, the switch tests hold near \((x_*,y_*)\), and the exact-Hessian SQP correction equals the primal–dual Newton correction.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Decomposed block updates for a coupled augmented Lagrangian
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider \(\min_{x_i\in X_i}\sum_{i=1}^N f_i(x_i)\) subject to \(\sum_{i=1}^N A_ix_i=b\). With \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\), define \(\mathcal L_\rho(x,\lambda)=\sum_i f_i(x_i)+\lambda^{\mathsf T}(\sum_iA_ix_i-b)+(\rho/2)\|\sum_iA_ix_i-b\|_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional separable objectives with a linear coupling constraint. The interface distinguishes joint augmented minimization from Jacobi or Gauss–Seidel block minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The decomposed multiplier interface replaces a joint update \(x^{k+1}\approx\arg\min_{x_i\in X_i}\mathcal L_{\rho_k}(x,\lambda^k)\) by block updates of the same augmented objective. A Jacobi update satisfies \(x_i^{k+1}\approx\arg\min_{u\in X_i}\mathcal L_{\rho_k}(x_1^k,\ldots,u,\ldots,x_N^k,\lambda^k)\) for all \(i\) in parallel. A Gauss–Seidel update uses new blocks \(x_j^{k+1}\) for \(j<i\) and old blocks \(x_j^k\) for \(j>i\). Both are followed by \(\lambda^{k+1}=\lambda^k+\rho_k(\sum_iA_ix_i^{k+1}-b)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a separable objective with a shared linear constraint, the augmented Lagrangian couples all blocks through one quadratic residual. Joint ALM minimizes over every block simultaneously. The decomposed interface instead minimizes that same coupled objective one block at a time, either in parallel using old blocks or sequentially using newly updated blocks, and then performs the common residual multiplier update.
assumptions_latex: Each \(X_i\) is nonempty and each \(f_i:X_i\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper.
The coupling maps \(A_i\) and vector \(b\) have compatible finite dimensions.
\(\rho_k>0\), and every approximate block minimization has a declared accuracy criterion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Decomposition is defined by Jacobi or Gauss–Seidel block minimization of the common coupled \(\mathcal L_{\rho_k}\), followed by the residual multiplier update.
equivalent_formulations_latex: With two blocks, the Gauss–Seidel form updates \(x_1\) using \(x_2^k\), then \(x_2\) using \(x_1^{k+1}\), then updates \(\lambda\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A_i=0\) for a block, its augmented subproblem decouples from the shared residual.
When \(N=1\), blockwise and joint augmented minimization coincide.
immediate_consequences_latex: The quadratic coupling generally prevents the joint augmented objective from being separable even when \(\sum_i f_i\) is separable.
Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel architectures are distinct because they condition block minimizers on different iterate states.
boundary_notes: Convergence is not implied by this definition; multi-block and parallel variants may require proximal terms or parameter restrictions.
Nonlinear coupling constraints require a different decomposed model.
The definition does not identify every block method with ADMM; additional update-order and problem-structure conditions are required.

notation.meaning: Linear map coupling block \(x_i\) to the shared constraint.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: blockwise Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel minimization of a coupled augmented objective precisely marks the decomposition interface.
No inspected source locator supports the full definition and its boundary with ADMM.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Method-of-Multipliers Baseline
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact joint method of multipliers for a two-block linearly constrained convex problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given the problem \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n,\,z\in\mathbb R^m} f(x)+g(z)\) subject to \(Ax+Bz=c\), choose \(\rho>0\) and \(y^0\in\mathbb R^p\). For \(k=0,1,\ldots\), compute a joint augmented-Lagrangian minimizer
\[
(x^{k+1},z^{k+1})\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R^n,\,z\in\mathbb R^m}\left\{f(x)+g(z)+\langle y^k,Ax+Bz-c\rangle+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert Ax+Bz-c\rVert^2\right\},
\]
and update \(y^{k+1}=y^k+\rho(Ax^{k+1}+Bz^{k+1}-c)\). Stop when prescribed primal-residual and multiplier-change tolerances hold; output \((x^{k+1},z^{k+1},y^{k+1})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a two-block convex problem with one affine coupling constraint, minimize the augmented Lagrangian jointly over both primal blocks and then update the multiplier by the penalty parameter times the constraint residual.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(g:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper, closed, convex functions.
\(A\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}\), \(B\in\mathbb R^{p\times m}\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y^{k+1}=y^k+\rho(Ax^{k+1}+Bz^{k+1}-c)\) is the method-of-multipliers dual update associated with the unsplit augmented subproblem.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h_1:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(h_2:\mathbb{R}^p\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper closed convex functions, let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p}\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^m\). The constrained problem is \(\min_{x,z}\{h_1(x)+h_2(z):Ax+Bz=c\}\), and its residual is \(r(x,z)=Ax+Bz-c\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the exact, deterministic, finite-dimensional equality-constrained method of multipliers with a joint primal minimization. It is the unsplit baseline against which alternating-direction updates are distinguished.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a penalty parameter \(\rho>0\), define the augmented Lagrangian by \[L_\rho(x,z;y)=h_1(x)+h_2(z)+\langle y,Ax+Bz-c\rangle+\frac{\rho}{2}\|Ax+Bz-c\|^2.\] Given \(y^0\in\mathbb{R}^m\), the joint method-of-multipliers iteration is the set-valued recursion, for every \(k\geq0\), \[(x^{k+1},z^{k+1})\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n,\,z\in\mathbb{R}^p}L_\rho(x,z;y^k),\qquad y^{k+1}=y^k+\rho(Ax^{k+1}+Bz^{k+1}-c).\] The word “joint” means that the pair \((x,z)\) solves one augmented subproblem; neither block is frozen at its preceding value during this minimization. The definition permits a nonunique primal minimizer, in which case any selected minimizer determines the subsequent multiplier update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the two-block convex problem \(\min h_1(x)+h_2(z)\) subject to \(Ax+Bz=c\), the joint method of multipliers forms \(L_\rho(x,z;y)=h_1(x)+h_2(z)+\langle y,Ax+Bz-c\rangle+(\rho/2)\|Ax+Bz-c\|^2\). At iteration \(k\), it minimizes this function simultaneously over both blocks, choosing \((x^{k+1},z^{k+1})\) from its joint argmin, and then sets \(y^{k+1}=y^k+\rho(Ax^{k+1}+Bz^{k+1}-c)\). Thus the complete coupled augmented subproblem is solved before the multiplier changes. The definition is set-valued when the joint minimizer is not unique.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Completing the square gives the same primal update as \[(x^{k+1},z^{k+1})\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x,z}\left\{h_1(x)+h_2(z)+\frac{\rho}{2}\left\|Ax+Bz-c+\frac{y^k}{\rho}\right\|^2\right\},\] because the omitted term \(-\|y^k\|^2/(2\rho)\) is independent of \((x,z)\).
special_cases_latex: With one primal block, for example \(B=0\), the definition reduces to \(x^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_x\{h_1(x)+\langle y^k,Ax-c\rangle+(\rho/2)\|Ax-c\|^2\}\) followed by \(y^{k+1}=y^k+\rho(Ax^{k+1}-c)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The multiplier increment is exactly the scaled new residual: \(y^{k+1}-y^k=\rho r(x^{k+1},z^{k+1})\). Hence a fixed point of the update has zero equality residual.
boundary_notes: This definition requires exact joint minimization; inexact augmented-Lagrangian subproblems require a separate error criterion.
Sequential minimization first in one block and then in the other is the alternating-direction interface, not this baseline.
Inequality constraints require multiplier-domain restrictions and projected or positive-part updates not included here.

children.title: Block-Separability Interface
children.top_down_role: Constraint and variable structures enabling decomposed augmented solution.

assumptions_latex: The equality is interpreted as an algebraic identity on the effective product domain of \(f\) and \(g\).
The residual norm is Euclidean, \(f\) depends only on \(x\), \(g\) depends only on \(z\), and \(\rho>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact criterion distinguishing conditional block minimizability from additive separability of the augmented subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mathcal L_\rho(x,z;y)=f(x)+g(z)+\langle y,Ax+Bz-c\rangle+(\rho/2)\lVert Ax+Bz-c\rVert^2\), expansion of the squared residual produces the mixed term \(\rho x^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}Bz\). Consequently, for fixed \(y\), \(\mathcal L_\rho\) is additively separable as \(\phi_y(x)+\psi_y(z)+\kappa_y\) for all \((x,z)\) if and only if \(A^{\mathsf T}B=0\). When \(A^{\mathsf T}B\ne0\), fixing one block still defines a conditional one-block subproblem, but the joint augmented minimization does not decompose into independent parallel minimizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separable objective does not by itself make the augmented subproblem separable: the quadratic coupling contributes a mixed term, which vanishes exactly when the two constraint blocks are orthogonal.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Term Separability Criterion
Block-Separability Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural condition exposing two proximal block subproblems under one linear coupling constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A problem has the two-block separability interface when its variables form a product \(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\), its objective is \(F(x,z)=f(x)+g(z)\), and its only cross-block constraint is \(Ax+Bz=c\). For every \(y\in\mathbb R^p\) and \(\rho>0\), fixing \(z\) reduces the augmented Lagrangian to a function of \(x\) alone, and fixing \(x\) reduces it to a function of \(z\) alone:
\[
\mathcal L_\rho(x,z;y)=f(x)+g(z)+\langle y,Ax+Bz-c\rangle+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert Ax+Bz-c\rVert^2.
\]
Thus alternating block minimization is well-defined whenever both conditional argmin sets are nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separable objective and affine cross-block constraint expose two conditional augmented-Lagrangian minimizations, provided both block minimizers exist.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper extended-real-valued functions on finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
\(A\) and \(B\) are linear maps with a common residual space.
The conditional augmented-Lagrangian minimizer sets are nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_x\mathcal L_\rho(x,z;y)\) and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_z\mathcal L_\rho(x,z;y)\) define separate block solution interfaces.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the block-separability leaf and is mathematically coherent, but no citation or inspectable locator supports the claimed decomposition interface.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\) be nonempty closed convex sets. Let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(g:Z\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper closed convex functions, and let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p}\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition concerns finite-dimensional two-block convex structure. It separates the objective and domains while allowing the equality constraint, and therefore the quadratic augmented term, to couple the blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linearly coupled problem has the two-block separability interface when it can be written as \[\min_{(x,z)\in X\times Z} f(x)+g(z)\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax+Bz=c.\] Separability means that the feasible domain before imposing the coupling equation is Cartesian and the objective is additively block-separable. For multiplier \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(\rho>0\), its augmented Lagrangian is \[L_\rho(x,z;y)=f(x)+g(z)+\langle y,Ax+Bz-c\rangle+\frac{\rho}{2}\|Ax+Bz-c\|^2.\] The ordinary Lagrangian terms remain block-separable, but the quadratic term contains the bilinear contribution \(\rho\langle Ax,Bz\rangle=\rho x^\mathsf{T}A^\mathsf{T}Bz\). Thus objective separability alone does not make the joint augmented subproblem decomposable. If \(A^\mathsf{T}B=0\), the bilinear contribution vanishes and, for fixed \(y\), the joint augmented minimization separates into independent minimizations over \(x\in X\) and \(z\in Z\). Without this orthogonality, fixing either block still produces a well-defined single-block augmented subproblem, which is the structural interface used by alternating-direction methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A problem has the two-block separability interface when its variables lie in a product set \(X\times Z\), its objective is \(f(x)+g(z)\), and its only cross-block relation is the linear equation \(Ax+Bz=c\). Its augmented Lagrangian adds a linear multiplier term and the squared residual penalty \((\rho/2)\|Ax+Bz-c\|^2\). Expanding that penalty exposes the cross term \(\rho x^\mathsf{T}A^\mathsf{T}Bz\), so a separable objective does not generally yield an independently solvable joint augmented subproblem. When \(A^\mathsf{T}B=0\), the cross term disappears and the joint minimization separates. In the general coupled case, one obtains a block subproblem by holding the other block fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interface is characterized by \(F(x,z)=f(x)+g(z)\), \((x,z)\in X\times Z\), and \(r(x,z)=Ax+Bz-c\); its sole quadratic cross-block term is \(\rho x^\mathsf{T}A^\mathsf{T}Bz\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Absorbing the set constraints into indicator functions gives the unconstrained-domain representation \[\min_{x,z}\bigl(f(x)+\delta_X(x)\bigr)+\bigl(g(z)+\delta_Z(z)\bigr)\quad\text{subject to}\quad Ax+Bz=c.\]
special_cases_latex: The consensus model \(x=z\) is obtained with \(A=I\), \(B=-I\), and \(c=0\); its objective may be separable even though its augmented penalty couples the two copies.
If \(B=0\), the \(z\)-block is absent from the coupling equation and its minimization is independent of the augmented residual.
immediate_consequences_latex: For fixed \((z,y)\), the \(x\)-subproblem depends only on \(f\), \(X\), \(A\), and the shifted residual \(Bz-c+y/\rho\); the symmetric statement holds for the \(z\)-subproblem.
When \(A^\mathsf{T}B=0\), the augmented objective is a sum of an \(x\)-only function, a \(z\)-only function, and a constant.
boundary_notes: Block separability does not assert that the original equality-constrained feasible set is Cartesian.
Orthogonality \(A^\mathsf{T}B=0\) is a sufficient algebraic condition for complete separation of the quadratic augmented subproblem; alternating minimization does not require it.
Multi-block Jacobi, Gauss-Seidel, and stochastic decompositions are nearby variants outside this two-block definition.

notation.meaning: Matrix controlling the bilinear cross term in the quadratic penalty.
Convex indicator functions of the block domains.

children.title: Alternating-Direction Interface
children.top_down_role: The transition from joint multiplier subproblems to alternating block minimization.

assumptions_latex: The problem has the form \(\min f(x)+g(z)\) subject to \(Ax+Bz=c\).
The two block updates satisfy their exact convex optimality inclusions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r^{k+1}=0\) and \(s^{k+1}=0\), together with the block optimality inclusions, give primal feasibility and stationarity with a common multiplier.

notation.meaning: dual residual induced by the second-block change

review_flags: dual residual depends on the chosen block-update ordering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical stopping residuals for the two-block affine-coupled alternating-direction method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the update order \(x\) then \(z\), define \(r^{k+1}=Ax^{k+1}+Bz^{k+1}-c\) and \(s^{k+1}=\rho A^{\mathsf T}B(z^{k+1}-z^k)\). The multiplier update gives \(y^{k+1}-y^k=\rho r^{k+1}\). The exact \(x\)-subproblem condition can be rewritten as \(0\in\partial f(x^{k+1})+A^{\mathsf T}y^{k+1}-s^{k+1}\), while the exact \(z\)-subproblem condition is \(0\in\partial g(z^{k+1})+B^{\mathsf T}y^{k+1}\). Thus small \(r^{k+1}\) and \(s^{k+1}\) measure affine infeasibility and the remaining mismatch between the two stationarity inclusions evaluated with the same multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal residual measures affine infeasibility, while the dual residual measures the stationarity mismatch caused by changing the second block after the first-block minimization.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal and Dual Residual Certificates

assumptions_latex: At least three primal blocks are updated cyclically by exact Gauss-Seidel minimization.
No additional strong-convexity, rank, proximal-regularization, correction, or stepsize hypothesis is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The assumptions sufficient for classical two-block ADMM do not ensure convergence of the direct cyclic multi-block extension.}
review_flags: concrete divergence family requires an authoritative locator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp limitation on transferring the classical two-block convergence result to a direct cyclic multi-block extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The direct cyclic extension that minimizes an augmented Lagrangian successively over three or more blocks and then performs one multiplier update is not covered by the classical two-block convergence theorem: finite-dimensional convex quadratic instances with linear coupling exist for which the unmodified multi-block iteration diverges. Convergence therefore requires additional structure or modification, such as suitable strong-convexity and rank conditions, proximal regularization, grouping into two blocks, or a corrected update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Naively extending the two-block alternating-direction iteration to three or more cyclically updated blocks can diverge even for convex quadratic problems.
knowledge_statements.title: Direct Multi-Block Extension Can Diverge

assumptions_latex: \(\rho>0\), and the displayed block minimizers exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scaled and unscaled iterations generate identical primal iterates and satisfy \(y^k=\rho u^k\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaled representation of the exact two-block alternating-direction iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r(x,z)=Ax+Bz-c\) and set \(u^k=y^k/\rho\). Completing the square gives \(\mathcal L_\rho(x,z;y^k)=f(x)+g(z)+(\rho/2)\lVert r(x,z)+u^k\rVert^2-(\rho/2)\lVert u^k\rVert^2\). Hence sequential minimization of \(\mathcal L_\rho\) is equivalently written as \(x^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_x\{f(x)+(\rho/2)\lVert Ax+Bz^k-c+u^k\rVert^2\}\), \(z^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_z\{g(z)+(\rho/2)\lVert Ax^{k+1}+Bz-c+u^k\rVert^2\}\), followed by \(u^{k+1}=u^k+Ax^{k+1}+Bz^{k+1}-c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dividing the multiplier by the penalty parameter yields the equivalent scaled ADMM form, in which each block minimizes a shifted squared residual and the scaled dual variable accumulates the primal residual.
knowledge_statements.title: Scaled Alternating-Direction Representation

assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper, closed, convex functions.
The unaugmented Lagrangian has a saddle point.
\(\rho>0\), both block subproblems are solved exactly, and the required minimizers exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r^k\to0,\quad s^k\to0,\quad f(x^k)+g(z^k)\to p_*,\quad y^k\to y_*\text{ for some dual solution }y_* .
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical convergence conclusion for exact two-block convex ADMM under saddle-point existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{f(x)+g(z):Ax+Bz=c\}\) and its exact two-block alternating-direction iteration with fixed \(\rho>0\). If \(f\) and \(g\) are proper, closed, and convex, the unaugmented Lagrangian has a saddle point, and every required block minimizer exists, then the primal residuals \(r^k=Ax^k+Bz^k-c\) and dual residuals \(s^k=\rho A^{\mathsf T}B(z^k-z^{k-1})\) converge to zero, the objective values converge to the primal optimum \(p_*\), and the multiplier sequence converges to a dual solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact two-block convex ADMM converges under saddle-point existence: feasibility and stationarity residuals vanish, objective values approach the optimum, and multipliers approach a dual solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Two-Block Convex Convergence
Alternating-Direction Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact two-block alternating-direction method obtained by replacing joint minimization with Gauss–Seidel block updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\min_{x,z} f(x)+g(z)\) subject to \(Ax+Bz=c\), choose \(\rho>0\), \(z^0\), and \(y^0\). For \(k=0,1,\ldots\), perform
\[
x^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_x\mathcal L_\rho(x,z^k;y^k),\qquad
z^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_z\mathcal L_\rho(x^{k+1},z;y^k),
\]
followed by \(y^{k+1}=y^k+\rho(Ax^{k+1}+Bz^{k+1}-c)\). Here \(\mathcal L_\rho(x,z;y)=f(x)+g(z)+\langle y,Ax+Bz-c\rangle+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert Ax+Bz-c\rVert^2\). Stop at specified primal- and dual-residual tolerances and return the latest primal-dual iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace the joint multiplier subproblem by sequential minimization over the first and second blocks, then apply the usual multiplier update.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper functions and \(Ax+Bz=c\) is dimensionally compatible.
Every displayed block argmin set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iteration is the exact two-block alternating-direction method of multipliers associated with \(\mathcal L_\rho\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm is the standard exact two-block ADMM iteration and fits the transition represented by this leaf, but it has no authoritative citation with a section, theorem, or page locator.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n,z\in\mathbb{R}^p}h_1(x)+h_2(z)\) subject to \(Ax+Bz=c\), where \(h_1\) and \(h_2\) are proper closed convex functions, \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p}\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^m\). Let \(L_\rho(x,z;y)=h_1(x)+h_2(z)+\langle y,Ax+Bz-c\rangle+(\rho/2)\|Ax+Bz-c\|^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the classical unrelaxed, unscaled, exact two-block ADMM in finite dimensions. The definition specifies the transition from one joint multiplier subproblem to sequential block minimizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x^0\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(z^0\in\mathbb{R}^p\), \(y^0\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(\rho>0\), the alternating direction method of multipliers is the recursion, for every \(k\geq0\), \[x^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}L_\rho(x,z^k;y^k),\] \[z^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in\mathbb{R}^p}L_\rho(x^{k+1},z;y^k),\] \[y^{k+1}=y^k+\rho(Ax^{k+1}+Bz^{k+1}-c).\] Equivalently, constants independent of the active block may be removed, giving \[x^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_x\left\{h_1(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\left\|Ax+Bz^k-c+\frac{y^k}{\rho}\right\|^2\right\},\] \[z^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_z\left\{h_2(z)+\frac{\rho}{2}\left\|Ax^{k+1}+Bz-c+\frac{y^k}{\rho}\right\|^2\right\}.\] The defining distinction from the joint method of multipliers is that the exact joint minimization of \(L_\rho(\cdot,\cdot;y^k)\) is replaced by one ordered alternating-minimization sweep before the same residual-based multiplier update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Classical two-block ADMM starts from \((x^0,z^0,y^0)\) and a positive penalty \(\rho\). It first minimizes the augmented Lagrangian over \(x\) while holding \(z=z^k\), then minimizes it over \(z\) using the new value \(x^{k+1}\), and finally updates the multiplier by \(y^{k+1}=y^k+\rho(Ax^{k+1}+Bz^{k+1}-c)\). This single ordered block sweep replaces the simultaneous augmented-Lagrangian minimization used by the joint method of multipliers. Either block update may be set-valued if its argmin is not unique.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: ADMM is the ordered update \[(x^{k+1},z^{k+1},y^{k+1})\in\bigl(\operatorname*{argmin}_xL_\rho(x,z^k;y^k),\operatorname*{argmin}_zL_\rho(x^{k+1},z;y^k),\,y^k+\rho r^{k+1}\bigr),\] where \(r^{k+1}=Ax^{k+1}+Bz^{k+1}-c\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: With the scaled dual variable \(u^k=y^k/\rho\), the multiplier update is \(u^{k+1}=u^k+Ax^{k+1}+Bz^{k+1}-c\), while the block objectives use the shifted residual \(Ax+Bz-c+u^k\).
special_cases_latex: For the consensus constraint \(x=z\), take \(A=I\), \(B=-I\), and \(c=0\); the two updates alternate between the two objective components with a quadratic agreement penalty.
If the joint augmented objective is already block-separable, one alternating sweep computes a joint minimizer and the ADMM primal step coincides with the joint method-of-multipliers step.
immediate_consequences_latex: The multiplier increment remains the scaled post-sweep primal residual: \(y^{k+1}-y^k=\rho r^{k+1}\).
The \(z\)-update uses \(x^{k+1}\), not \(x^k\); this Gauss-Seidel dependency is part of the classical alternating-direction definition.
boundary_notes: The definition does not include relaxation, over-relaxation, proximal regularizers, linearized subproblems, or inexact block solves.
Existence of both block argmins is required for the recursion to be well defined; proper closed convexity alone does not guarantee attainment for arbitrary matrices.
A simultaneous Jacobi update of both blocks is not classical two-block ADMM.

children.title: Proximal Operator Interface
children.top_down_role: The boundary between multiplier methods, proximal regularization, and monotone inclusions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(\gamma>0\). Its convex subdifferential is the set-valued operator \(\partial f:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the Euclidean finite-dimensional proximal operator. It identifies the exact boundary between quadratic proximal regularization and the resolvent of a maximal monotone subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The proximal operator of \(\gamma f\) is the single-valued map \[\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n,\qquad \operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}(v)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{f(x)+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\|x-v\|^2\right\}.\] Equivalently, multiplying the objective by \(\gamma\) yields \[\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}(v)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{\gamma f(x)+\frac12\|x-v\|^2\right\}.\] The quadratic term makes the objective strongly convex, so the minimizer exists and is unique for every \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Its defining optimality inclusion is \[0\in\partial f(x)+\frac{1}{\gamma}(x-v),\] which is equivalent to \(v\in x+\gamma\partial f(x)\). Consequently, \[\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}=(I+\gamma\partial f)^{-1}=J_{\gamma\partial f}.\] Thus a proximal evaluation is exactly a backward, or resolvent, step for the monotone inclusion generated by \(\partial f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function \(f\) and \(\gamma>0\), the proximal operator sends each \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\) to the unique minimizer of \(f(x)+(1/(2\gamma))\|x-v\|^2\). The same point satisfies \(0\in\partial f(x)+(x-v)/\gamma\), or equivalently \(v\in(I+\gamma\partial f)(x)\). Hence the proximal operator is the resolvent \((I+\gamma\partial f)^{-1}\) of the subdifferential. This equality is the formal interface between proximal regularization and monotone-operator methods.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[x=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}(v)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{v-x}{\gamma}\in\partial f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=J_{\gamma\partial f}(v).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The Moreau envelope associated with the same minimization is \(e_\gamma f(v)=\min_x\{f(x)+(1/(2\gamma))\|x-v\|^2\}\), and its minimizer is \(\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}(v)\).
special_cases_latex: For the indicator \(f=\delta_C\) of a nonempty closed convex set \(C\), \(\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}=\Pi_C\), the Euclidean projection, independently of \(\gamma\).
For \(f(x)=\|x\|_1\), the proximal operator is componentwise soft thresholding at level \(\gamma\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Because \(\partial f\) is maximal monotone, \(J_{\gamma\partial f}\) has full domain and is firmly nonexpansive.
A point \(x^\star\) minimizes \(f\) exactly when \(x^\star=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}(x^\star)\).
boundary_notes: For nonconvex functions the proximal mapping may be empty or multivalued; that regime is excluded.
Variable-metric and Bregman proximal maps replace the Euclidean quadratic and are not covered by this definition.
The scaling conventions \(\gamma f(x)+(1/2)\|x-v\|^2\) and \(f(x)+(1/(2\gamma))\|x-v\|^2\) are equivalent but should not be mixed with the convention \(f(x)+(\gamma/2)\|x-v\|^2\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean proximal operator of the scaled function \(\gamma f\).

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Proximal-Point Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact equality-constrained ALM as proximal-point maximization of the concave dual function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(q(y)=\inf_x\{f(x)+\langle y,Ax-b\rangle\}\). If
\[
x^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_x\left\{f(x)+\langle y^k,Ax-b\rangle+\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert Ax-b\rVert^2\right\},
\qquad y^{k+1}=y^k+\rho(Ax^{k+1}-b),
\]
then the multiplier update satisfies
\[
y^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in\mathbb R^p}\left\{q(y)-\frac{1}{2\rho}\lVert y-y^k\rVert^2\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, with the convex function \(h=-q\), one has \(y^{k+1}=(I+\rho\,\partial h)^{-1}(y^k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact augmented-Lagrangian multiplier update is a proximal-point step maximizing the concave dual function.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex.
The affine-constrained primal problem has a saddle point.
The augmented primal subproblem attains its minimum.

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of the negative dual function
identity mapping on the multiplier space

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regularized dual is the negative Moreau envelope of the negative dual function, and its gradient is the affine-feasibility residual generated by the exact augmented-Lagrangian minimizer.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Method of multipliers as dual proximal-point iteration
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper closed convex, let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\). For \(\min_x\{f(x):Ax=b\}\), define the concave dual function \(q(y)=\inf_x\{f(x)+\langle y,Ax-b\rangle\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the exact finite-dimensional equality-constrained convex correspondence. It uses the concave maximization form of the dual and the same positive parameter in the primal quadratic penalty and dual proximal term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\rho>0\), the dual proximal-point update at \(y^k\in\mathbb{R}^m\) is \[y^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in\mathbb{R}^m}\left\{q(y)-\frac{1}{2\rho}\|y-y^k\|^2\right\}.\] The associated method-of-multipliers realization is \[x^{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{f(x)+\langle y^k,Ax-b\rangle+\frac{\rho}{2}\|Ax-b\|^2\right\},\] \[y^{k+1}=y^k+\rho(Ax^{k+1}-b).\] Whenever the displayed primal minimizer and dual proximal maximizer are attained under the standard convex duality hypotheses, these formulas define the same multiplier \(y^{k+1}\). Equivalently, with the convex function \(F=-q\), the multiplier step is the ordinary proximal evaluation \(y^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\rho F}(y^k)\). This identity is the dual regularization interface: minimizing a primal augmented Lagrangian implements a proximal-point step on the negative dual objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the equality-constrained convex problem \(\min f(x)\) subject to \(Ax=b\), let \(q\) be its concave dual function. A dual proximal-point step maximizes \(q(y)-(1/(2\rho))\|y-y^k\|^2\). The method of multipliers computes the same new multiplier by minimizing the primal augmented Lagrangian at \(y^k\) and then setting \(y^{k+1}=y^k+\rho(Ax^{k+1}-b)\). In convex minimization notation, this is \(y^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\rho(-q)}(y^k)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The dual proximal-point and multiplier updates coincide as \[\operatorname*{argmax}_y\left\{q(y)-\frac{1}{2\rho}\|y-y^k\|^2\right\}\ni y^{k+1}=y^k+\rho(Ax^{k+1}-b),\] where \(x^{k+1}\) minimizes the augmented Lagrangian at \(y^k\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Writing \(F=-q\) gives \[y^{k+1}=\operatorname*{argmin}_y\left\{F(y)+\frac{1}{2\rho}\|y-y^k\|^2\right\}=\operatorname{prox}_{\rho F}(y^k).\]
In resolvent notation, \(y^{k+1}=(I+\rho\partial(-q))^{-1}(y^k)\) whenever \(-q\) is proper closed convex.
special_cases_latex: For convex inequality constraints, the dual proximal maximization is restricted to the nonnegative orthant, and the multiplier update becomes a componentwise positive-part projection.
If \(A=I\) and \(b=0\), the residual update directly regularizes the dual of the constraint \(x=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The multiplier displacement encodes the primal residual: \((y^{k+1}-y^k)/\rho=Ax^{k+1}-b\).
The dual proximal objective is strongly concave because of the quadratic term, so its maximizer is unique when it exists.
boundary_notes: The correspondence stated here is exact; inexact augmented-Lagrangian minimization corresponds to an inexact proximal-point step and requires an explicit error condition.
For inequality constraints, omitting the dual-domain restriction changes the method.
Nonconvex local augmented-Lagrangian methods do not generally admit this global convex dual proximal interpretation.

notation.meaning: Convex negative-dual objective used by proximal minimization.
Both the primal quadratic-penalty parameter and the dual proximal stepsize.

children.title: Resolvent and Operator-Splitting Views
children.top_down_role: The operator-theoretic route from multiplier methods to splitting algorithms.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal{H}=\mathbb{R}^n\) with its Euclidean inner product. Let \(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}:\mathcal{H}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{H}\) be maximal monotone operators, let \(\gamma>0\), and consider the inclusion \(0\in(\mathcal{A}+\mathcal{B})(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This is the finite-dimensional two-operator Douglas–Rachford resolvent interface, together with its convex-subdifferential and ADMM interpretations. It does not assert a convergence theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a set-valued operator \(\mathcal{A}\), its scaled resolvent and reflected resolvent are \[J_{\gamma\mathcal{A}}=(I+\gamma\mathcal{A})^{-1},\qquad R_{\gamma\mathcal{A}}=2J_{\gamma\mathcal{A}}-I.\] The Douglas–Rachford splitting operator for the ordered pair \((\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})\) is \[T_{\mathrm{DR}}=\frac12\left(I+R_{\gamma\mathcal{A}}R_{\gamma\mathcal{B}}\right).\] Its fixed-point iteration may be written \[x^{k+1/2}=J_{\gamma\mathcal{B}}(z^k),\qquad x^{k+1}=J_{\gamma\mathcal{A}}(2x^{k+1/2}-z^k),\qquad z^{k+1}=z^k+x^{k+1}-x^{k+1/2}.\] The resolvent-splitting correspondence is \[z\in\operatorname{Fix}(T_{\mathrm{DR}})\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=J_{\gamma\mathcal{B}}(z)\ \text{and}\ 0\in(\mathcal{A}+\mathcal{B})(x),\] with the converse fixed-point representation holding for solutions through an appropriate preimage \(z\). If \(\mathcal{A}=\partial f\) and \(\mathcal{B}=\partial g\) for proper closed convex functions, then the resolvents are proximal operators. Applied to the Fenchel dual of a two-block linearly constrained convex program, this splitting yields the classical ADMM iteration after the standard identification of the dual and shadow variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For maximal monotone operators \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{B}\), the resolvent is \(J_{\gamma\mathcal{A}}=(I+\gamma\mathcal{A})^{-1}\), and the reflected resolvent is \(R_{\gamma\mathcal{A}}=2J_{\gamma\mathcal{A}}-I\). Douglas–Rachford splitting averages the identity with the composition of the two reflected resolvents. A fixed point \(z\) produces a solution of \(0\in(\mathcal{A}+\mathcal{B})(x)\) through the shadow value \(x=J_{\gamma\mathcal{B}}z\). When the operators are convex subdifferentials, these resolvents are proximal maps. Applying this construction to the dual inclusion of a two-block linearly constrained convex problem gives ADMM after variable identification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The correspondence is \[T_{\mathrm{DR}}=\frac12(I+R_{\gamma\mathcal{A}}R_{\gamma\mathcal{B}}),\qquad z\in\operatorname{Fix}(T_{\mathrm{DR}})\Longleftrightarrow\left(J_{\gamma\mathcal{B}}z\in\operatorname{Zer}(\mathcal{A}+\mathcal{B})\right),\] with the reverse direction understood through the associated fixed-point preimage.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Expanding the reflected resolvents gives \[T_{\mathrm{DR}}=I-J_{\gamma\mathcal{B}}+J_{\gamma\mathcal{A}}(2J_{\gamma\mathcal{B}}-I).\]
For \(\mathcal{A}=\partial f\) and \(\mathcal{B}=\partial g\), \(J_{\gamma\mathcal{A}}=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}\) and \(J_{\gamma\mathcal{B}}=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\mathcal{B}=N_C\), the normal cone of a nonempty closed convex set \(C\), then \(J_{\gamma\mathcal{B}}=\Pi_C\), so every shadow iterate \(x^{k+1/2}\) lies in \(C\).
Replacing the average by the unaveraged composition \(R_{\gamma\mathcal{A}}R_{\gamma\mathcal{B}}\) gives Peaceman–Rachford splitting rather than Douglas–Rachford splitting.
immediate_consequences_latex: The fixed-point variable \(z\) need not itself solve the original inclusion; the solution is the resolvent shadow \(J_{\gamma\mathcal{B}}z\).
The ADMM connection is a dual splitting correspondence, whereas the joint method of multipliers is a dual proximal-point correspondence.
boundary_notes: The order of \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{B}\) affects the shadow-variable representation even though both orders target the same sum inclusion.
The displayed correspondence is for two maximal monotone operators; forward-backward and three-operator splittings use different operators and assumptions.

ADMM equivalence requires forming the appropriate dual inclusion and identifying variables; it is not the assertion that arbitrary primal ADMM iterates equal arbitrary Douglas–Rachford iterates without transformation.

children.title: Resolvent Formulations
children.top_down_role: Resolvent-based representations associated with multiplier and proximal constructions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of maximal monotonicity through the resolvent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\gamma>0\), a maximally monotone operator \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\) has an everywhere-defined firmly nonexpansive resolvent: \(\|J_{\gamma T}x-J_{\gamma T}y\|^2\le\langle J_{\gamma T}x-J_{\gamma T}y,x-y\rangle\). Conversely, every everywhere-defined firmly nonexpansive map \(F:H\to H\) is the resolvent of the maximally monotone operator \(T=\gamma^{-1}(F^{-1}-I)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Resolvents of maximally monotone operators are exactly the everywhere-defined firmly nonexpansive mappings, and the underlying operator can be reconstructed from its resolvent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\text{ is maximally monotone}\Longleftrightarrow J_{\gamma T}\text{ is everywhere defined and firmly nonexpansive}.\)

notation.meaning: set-valued inverse relation of the mapping F

knowledge_statements.title: Firm Nonexpansiveness and Minty Reconstruction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-analytic specialization connecting resolvents to proximal minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, then \(J_{\gamma\partial f}(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in H}\{f(u)+(2\gamma)^{-1}\|u-x\|^2\}=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}(x)\). The unique minimizer satisfies \(0\in\partial f(u)+\gamma^{-1}(u-x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The resolvent of a convex subdifferential is the proximal mapping, and its resolvent inclusion is the proximal optimality condition.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferential Resolvents as Proximal Maps

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between firm nonexpansiveness of a resolvent and nonexpansiveness of its reflection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:H\to H\) and define \(R=2F-I\). Then
\[F\text{ is firmly nonexpansive}\iff R\text{ is nonexpansive}.\]
Consequently, if \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone and \(\gamma>0\), then \(R_{\gamma T}=2J_{\gamma T}-I\) is nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reflecting a firmly nonexpansive resolvent produces a nonexpansive mapping, exactly the property used by reflection-based splitting methods.

notation.meaning: reflected resolvent of the scaled operator

knowledge_statements.title: Reflected-Resolvent Nonexpansiveness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact fixed-point certificate for zeros of a maximally monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone and \(\gamma>0\). Then \[x\in\operatorname{zer}T\iff J_{\gamma T}x=x\iff R_{\gamma T}x=x.\] Hence zeros of \(T\) are exactly the fixed points of both its resolvent and its reflected resolvent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point solves the monotone inclusion exactly when it is fixed by the resolvent, equivalently by the reflected resolvent.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Resolvent Fixed Points Equal Operator Zeros
knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Fixed Points Equal Operator Zeros

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-valued regularization of a maximally monotone operator induced by its resolvent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone and \(\gamma>0\). Define \[T_\gamma=\gamma^{-1}(I-J_{\gamma T}).\] Then, for every \(x\in H\), \[T_\gamma x\in T(J_{\gamma T}x),\qquad x=J_{\gamma T}x+\gamma T_\gamma x.\] The map \(T_\gamma\) is single-valued, monotone, and \(1/\gamma\)-Lipschitz, and \[T_\gamma x=0\iff x\in\operatorname{zer}T.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The resolvent decomposes a point into an implicit operator point and a scaled single-valued Yosida value while preserving zeros.
knowledge_statements.title: Yosida Approximation Representation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Resolvent Decomposition for an Inverse Operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized Moreau decomposition relating the resolvents of a maximally monotone operator and its inverse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone and let \(\gamma>0\). Then for every \(x\in H\), \[J_{\gamma T}(x)+\gamma J_{\gamma^{-1}T^{-1}}(x/\gamma)=x.\] Equivalently, \[I-J_{\gamma T}=\gamma J_{\gamma^{-1}T^{-1}}\circ(\gamma^{-1}I).\] For \(T=\partial f\), this specializes to the Moreau decomposition involving \(\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}\) and the correspondingly scaled proximal map of \(f^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point decomposes into the resolvent component of an operator and a scaled resolvent component of its inverse, generalizing Moreau decomposition.

notation.meaning: inverse relation of the operator T
resolvent of the scaled inverse operator

knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Decomposition for an Inverse Operator

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric specialization of resolvents to closed convex feasibility sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset H\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(N_C\) be its convex normal-cone operator. For every \(\gamma>0\), \[J_{\gamma N_C}=P_C,\qquad R_{\gamma N_C}=2P_C-I,\] where \(P_C\) is the metric projection onto \(C\). Equivalently, \[p=P_Cx\iff x-p\in N_C(p).\] The resolvent is independent of the positive scaling \(\gamma\) because \(N_C(p)\) is a cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The resolvent of a convex normal cone is the metric projection, and its reflected resolvent is reflection across the set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Resolvents as Projections

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximality Is Needed for a Globally Defined Resolvent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp domain failure when a monotone operator is not maximally monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\mathbb R\) and define \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\) by \(T(0)=\{0\}\) and \(T(x)=\varnothing\) for \(x\ne0\). Then \(T\) is monotone but not maximally monotone. For every \(\gamma>0\), \[\operatorname{ran}(I+\gamma T)=\{0\},\qquad J_{\gamma T}(0)=0,\] while \(J_{\gamma T}(x)=\varnothing\) for \(x\ne0\). Thus monotonicity alone does not make the resolvent everywhere defined; maximal monotonicity supplies the global range property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone but nonmaximal operator can have a resolvent defined at only one point, so monotonicity alone does not guarantee a global implicit update.

notation.meaning: range of the shifted set-valued operator
domain on which the resolvent has a value

knowledge_statements.title: Maximality Is Needed for a Globally Defined Resolvent

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strengthened regularity of the single-valued operator induced by a maximally monotone resolvent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone, let \(\gamma>0\), and define \(T_\gamma=\gamma^{-1}(I-J_{\gamma T})\). Then, for all \(x,y\in H\), \[\langle T_\gamma x-T_\gamma y,x-y\rangle\geq\gamma\|T_\gamma x-T_\gamma y\|^2.\] Thus \(T_\gamma\) is \(\gamma\)-cocoercive and consequently monotone and \(1/\gamma\)-Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Yosida approximation of a maximally monotone operator is gamma-cocoercive, which implies monotonicity and reciprocal-gamma Lipschitz continuity.
knowledge_statements.title: Cocoercivity of the Yosida Approximation
Resolvent Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolvent and reflected-resolvent notation for a set-valued operator on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\), and let \(\gamma>0\). The resolvent and reflected resolvent of \(T\) are
\[
J_{\gamma T}:=(I+\gamma T)^{-1},\qquad R_{\gamma T}:=2J_{\gamma T}-I.
\]
For \(x,p\in H\), the resolvent relation is
\[
p\in J_{\gamma T}(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-p\in\gamma T(p).
\]
If \(T\) is maximally monotone, then \(J_{\gamma T}\) is everywhere defined and single-valued; hence \(R_{\gamma T}\) is also an everywhere-defined mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The resolvent converts an operator inclusion into an implicit update; maximal monotonicity makes this update single-valued and globally defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p=J_{\gamma T}(x)\) exactly when \(0\in T(p)+\gamma^{-1}(p-x)\); maximal monotonicity makes this point unique.

notation.meaning: identity operator on the Hilbert space

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The resolvent definitions and maximal-monotonicity property fit this definition container and are standard, but the record supplies no authoritative source or specific locator.

children.title: Operator-Splitting Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Connections from augmented multiplier structures to operator-splitting families.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic convergence guarantee for the two-resolvent Douglas–Rachford interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_{\mathrm{DR}}=\tfrac12(I+R_{\gamma B}R_{\gamma A})\), \(w^{k+1}=T_{\mathrm{DR}}w^k\), and \(p^k=J_{\gamma A}w^k\). If \(A\) and \(B\) are maximally monotone and \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\ne\varnothing\), then \(w^k\rightharpoonup\bar w\in\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{DR}}\), \(w^k-T_{\mathrm{DR}}w^k\to0\), and \(p^k\rightharpoonup J_{\gamma A}\bar w\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\). In finite-dimensional spaces these convergences are strong.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Douglas–Rachford iterates converge weakly to a fixed point, their displacement vanishes, and their shadows converge to a zero of the summed inclusion; finite-dimensional convergence is strong.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w^k\rightharpoonup\bar w\in\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{DR}}\) and \(J_{\gamma A}w^k\rightharpoonup J_{\gamma A}\bar w\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Douglas–Rachford Weak Convergence

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Douglas–Rachford Displacement Is Not Generally a Pointwise Sum Residual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limitation of the standard resolvent-discrepancy stopping quantity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a Douglas\text{–}Rachford step
\[p=J_{\gamma A}w,\qquad q=J_{\gamma B}(2p-w),\]
one has
\[a:=\gamma^{-1}(w-p)\in A(p),\qquad b:=\gamma^{-1}(2p-w-q)\in B(q),\qquad a+b=\gamma^{-1}(p-q).\]
Thus \(\|p-q\|\) measures cancellation between an \(A\)-value at \(p\) and a \(B\)-value at \(q\). Unless \(p=q\), or additional continuity or error-bound assumptions transfer \(B(q)\) to \(B(p)\), it is not by itself a pointwise residual \(\operatorname{dist}(0,(A+B)(p))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Douglas–Rachford displacement combines operator values evaluated at different points, so a small displacement is not automatically a small summed-inclusion residual at the shadow point.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(B\) are operators on a real Hilbert space.
The displayed resolvent evaluations are well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: a+b=\gamma^{-1}(p-q)\text{ with }a\in A(p),\ b\in B(q),\text{ but generally }\gamma^{-1}(p-q)\notin(A+B)(p).

notation.meaning: Douglas–Rachford fixed-point displacement up to sign
operator values recovered from the two resolvent evaluations

knowledge_statements.title: Douglas–Rachford Displacement Is Not Generally a Pointwise Sum Residual

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best-iterate complexity of the computable Douglas–Rachford displacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_{\mathrm{DR}}=\tfrac12(I+R_{\gamma B}R_{\gamma A})\), suppose \(\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{DR}}\ne\varnothing\), and set \(w^{k+1}=T_{\mathrm{DR}}w^k\). For every \(w^\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{DR}}\), \[\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\|w^k-T_{\mathrm{DR}}w^k\|^2\le\|w^0-w^\star\|^2.\] Hence \[\min_{0\le k<K}\|w^k-T_{\mathrm{DR}}w^k\|\le\frac{\operatorname{dist}(w^0,\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{DR}})}{\sqrt K}.\] In the two-resolvent implementation, \(w^k-T_{\mathrm{DR}}w^k=p^k-q^k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The best Douglas–Rachford displacement among the first K steps is at most the initial fixed-point distance divided by the square root of K.
review_flags: The displacement is a fixed-point residual, not generally \(\operatorname{dist}(0,(A+B)(p^k))\).
knowledge_statements.title: Douglas–Rachford Fixed-Point Displacement Rate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxed two-resolvent variant of the Douglas–Rachford operator interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For maximally monotone \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\), \(\gamma>0\), and \(0<\theta<2\), compute \[p^k=J_{\gamma A}w^k,\qquad q^k=J_{\gamma B}(2p^k-w^k),\qquad w^{k+1}=w^k+\theta(q^k-p^k).\] If \(T_{\mathrm{DR}}=\tfrac12(I+R_{\gamma B}R_{\gamma A})\), then \[w^{k+1}=((1-\theta)I+\theta T_{\mathrm{DR}})w^k.\] The standard Douglas–Rachford step is the special case \(\theta=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxed Douglas–Rachford scales the standard fixed-point displacement by a factor strictly between zero and two.
review_flags: This is the relaxed variant; the immutable deferred seed remains the canonical unrelaxed algorithm record.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxed Douglas–Rachford Interface

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak convergence of the relaxed two-resolvent interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone, suppose \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\neq\varnothing\), and generate the relaxed Douglas–Rachford sequence with fixed \(0<\theta<2\). Then \((1-\theta)I+\theta T_{\mathrm{DR}}\) is averaged, \(w^k\rightharpoonup\bar w\in\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{DR}}\), and \(p^k-q^k\to0\). Moreover, \[p^k=J_{\gamma A}w^k\rightharpoonup J_{\gamma A}\bar w\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B).\] In finite-dimensional spaces these convergences are strong.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every fixed relaxation strictly between zero and two preserves Douglas–Rachford convergence to a fixed point and convergence of its shadow to a solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: w^k\rightharpoonup\bar w\in\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{DR}},\qquad J_{\gamma A}w^k\rightharpoonup J_{\gamma A}\bar w\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B).

notation.meaning: the two relaxed Douglas–Rachford resolvent evaluations

knowledge_statements.title: Convergence of Relaxed Douglas–Rachford Splitting

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure of the relaxed Douglas–Rachford convergence range at relaxation parameter two.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\mathbb R^2\), let \(U\) be the horizontal axis, and let \(V\) be a line making an angle \(\alpha\in(0,\pi/2)\) with \(U\), where \(\alpha/\pi\) is irrational. Set \(A=N_U\), \(B=N_V\), and \(\gamma>0\). Then \(J_{\gamma A}=P_U\), \(J_{\gamma B}=P_V\), and the relaxed Douglas\text{–}Rachford update with \(\theta=2\) is \[w^{k+1}=R_VR_Uw^k.\] The map \(R_VR_U\) is rotation through angle \(2\alpha\). Therefore every nonzero orbit stays on a circle and fails to converge, although \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)=U\cap V=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At relaxation two, Douglas–Rachford becomes Peaceman–Rachford; two subspace reflections can rotate forever despite existence of a solution.
assumptions_latex: \(U,V\subset\mathbb R^2\) are distinct lines meeting at the origin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: w^{k+1}=R_VR_Uw^k\text{ need not converge even though }\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\neq\varnothing.

notation.meaning: normal-cone operators of the two subspaces
orthogonal reflections across U and V

knowledge_statements.title: Peaceman–Rachford Endpoint Need Not Converge
Operator-Splitting Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Douglas–Rachford resolvent splitting for a sum of two maximally monotone operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given maximally monotone operators \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\), a parameter \(\gamma>0\), and \(w^0\in H\), iterate
\[
p^k=J_{\gamma A}(w^k),\qquad q^k=J_{\gamma B}(2p^k-w^k),\qquad w^{k+1}=w^k+q^k-p^k.
\]
Equivalently, \(w^{k+1}=T_{\mathrm{DR}}w^k\), where
\[
T_{\mathrm{DR}}=\frac12\bigl(I+R_{\gamma B}R_{\gamma A}\bigr).
\]
Stop when \(\lVert p^k-q^k\rVert\) meets a prescribed tolerance and output the shadow point \(p^k\), which is an approximate zero of \(A+B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Douglas–Rachford splitting alternates two resolvents and updates an auxiliary point; the resolvent discrepancy is the inclusion residual.
assumptions_latex: \(\gamma>0\), and the zero set \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iteration uses only separate evaluations of \(J_{\gamma A}\) and \(J_{\gamma B}\), while its fixed-point shadows target \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\).

notation.meaning: set of points satisfying the summed inclusion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact correspondence between Douglas–Rachford fixed points and zeros of the summed inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_{\mathrm{DR}}=\tfrac12(I+R_{\gamma B}R_{\gamma A})\). If \(w\in\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{DR}}\), set \(p=J_{\gamma A}w\) and \(a=\gamma^{-1}(w-p)\). Then \[a\in A(p),\qquad -a\in B(p),\qquad 0\in(A+B)(p).\] Conversely, if \(p\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\) and \(a\in A(p)\cap(-B(p))\), then \(w=p+\gamma a\) belongs to \(\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{DR}}\) and \(J_{\gamma A}w=p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Douglas–Rachford fixed point lifts a zero of the summed inclusion together with cancelling operator values, and every such zero-and-value pair generates a fixed point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Douglas–Rachford Displacement as a Split Graph Residual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact relation between fixed-point displacement, resolvent discrepancy, and graph values evaluated at two shadow points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(w\in H\), set \(p=J_{\gamma A}w\), \(q=J_{\gamma B}(2p-w)\), \(a=\gamma^{-1}(w-p)\in A(p)\), and \(b=\gamma^{-1}(2p-w-q)\in B(q)\). Then \(w-T_{\mathrm{DR}}w=p-q=\gamma(a+b)\). Thus zero displacement implies \(p=q\) and \(0\in A(p)+B(p)\). Away from a fixed point, \(a\) and \(b\) are generally evaluated at different points, so \(\|p-q\|\) is a fixed-point or split-graph residual, not by itself a same-point residual for \(A+B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Douglas–Rachford displacement equals the shadow discrepancy and a sum of graph values evaluated at two shadow points; only zero displacement makes these a same-point zero of the operator sum.

notation.meaning: operator graph values induced by the two resolvent evaluations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact parametrization of fixed points by primal zeros and compatible graph values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T_{\mathrm{DR}}=\tfrac12(I+R_{\gamma B}R_{\gamma A})\). Then
\[
\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{DR}}=\{p+\gamma a:\ a\in A(p),\ -a\in B(p)\}.
\]
Thus the fixed points over \(p\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\) form the fiber \(p+\gamma(A(p)\cap[-B(p)])\), which need not be a singleton even when the primal zero is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Douglas–Rachford fixed points are primal zeros shifted by compatible opposing graph values; a unique primal zero can have multiple fixed-point representatives.

notation.meaning: compatible graph values whose sum is zero at p
fixed-point fiber above the primal zero p

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unique Zero with a Nontrivial Fixed-Point Fiber
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of uniqueness transfer from primal zeros to Douglas–Rachford fixed points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(H=\mathbb R\), let \(A=N_{[0,\infty)}\) and \(B=N_{(-\infty,0]}\). Then \(\operatorname{zer}(A+B)=\{0\}\), but for every \(\gamma>0\),
\[
\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{DR}}=(-\infty,0].
\]
Indeed, \(A(0)=(-\infty,0]\), \(-B(0)=(-\infty,0]\), so the fixed-point fiber above the unique zero is \(0+\gamma(-\infty,0]=(-\infty,0]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two opposing normal-cone operators have a unique primal zero but infinitely many Douglas–Rachford fixed points.

notation.meaning: normal-cone operator of the closed convex set C

knowledge_statements.title: Unique Zero with a Nontrivial Fixed-Point Fiber
Resolvent–Splitting Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-point representation of zeros of an operator sum through reflected resolvents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone and \(\gamma>0\), and define
\[
T_{\mathrm{DR}}=\frac12\bigl(I+R_{\gamma B}R_{\gamma A}\bigr).
\]
Then the zeros of the summed inclusion are precisely the resolvent shadows of Douglas–Rachford fixed points:
\[
\operatorname{zer}(A+B)=J_{\gamma A}\bigl(\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{DR}}\bigr).
\]
More explicitly, if \(w\in\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{DR}}\) and \(p=J_{\gamma A}w\), then \(0\in A(p)+B(p)\). Conversely, each \(p\in\operatorname{zer}(A+B)\) has at least one associated \(w\in\operatorname{Fix}T_{\mathrm{DR}}\) satisfying \(p=J_{\gamma A}w\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zeros of a two-operator sum are exactly the resolvent shadows of Douglas–Rachford fixed points.

notation.meaning: fixed-point set of the Douglas–Rachford operator
zero set of the operator sum
shadow map from fixed points to primal zeros
